title: Warlock of Firetop Mountain - Take a Look
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GqAXRVF_edY

Daniel (@dungeondive) reads the opening paragraph of Steve Jackson and Ian Livingstone's gamebook aloud before turning to the object itself: the 1986 Games Workshop board game of *The Warlock of Firetop Mountain*, and a verdict he reaches early and does not soften.

The character sheets are a faithful reproduction of the gamebook's — Skill, Stamina and Luck rolled at the start, a lantern and a sword — but the plastic figure you choose means nothing mechanically. You roll and move, one space at a time, through rooms seeded at random with one encounter and one treasure each: monsters resolved on 2d6 plus Skill, spike traps, a hex master who will curse a rival for two gold. The Eye of the Cyclops kills Zagor without a fight.

The stranger half is a *Clue*-style deduction layer. Three keys open the final chest, and key challenges force other players to reveal or bluff, so you are working out by elimination which keys nobody holds. Daniel finds it unintuitive, thinks the game too long for what it offers, and says the solo variants strip out the player-versus-player scheming that is the only real engine here. What he does praise, twice, is the map — a genuinely good board-game dungeon that deserves a better game around it.

----

When a mediocre game has one excellent component, is it worth keeping for parts — or does that map deserve to be cannibalised into something else?
